entries.notes: Today's BYOO-lunt stresses the first syllable. ü → 'oo' (guide; Hüseyin). The [æ] is Turkish /e/ lowered before l; written 'e' as in Mehmet.

entries.name: Hamada
entries.source: Egyptian Arabic حمادة (ḥamāda): stress on the long ā (Arabic stress rule)
entries.notes: GB-only fix: British today says hɒmˈɒdə, the 'lot' vowel for the long ā (Khalid, Adi precedents). US already right.

entries.name: Omid
entries.source: Wiktionary, Persian امید (omid): Iran formal [ʔo.míːd̪̥]; Behind the Name /ʔo.ˈmiːd/
entries.notes: Matches n0019. Today's oh-MID shortens the long ī.

entries.name: Rishi
entries.source: Wikipedia, Rishi Sunak: /ˈrɪʃi/
entries.notes: Ordinary word 'rishi' (a Hindu sage). The name sounds the same (RISH-ee, today's reading), so nothing needs to ship.

entries.name: Katarzyna
entries.source: Wiktionary, Polish Katarzyna: /ka.taˈʐɘ.na/
entries.notes: Polish rz is zh and y [ɘ] is the 'bit' vowel; today's kah-tur-ZIN-uh reads rz as r + z.

entries.name: Mubashir
entries.source: Urdu/Arabic مبشر (mubashshir): short u, short a, geminate sh; the heavy middle syllable takes the stress (Arabic and Hindustani rules agree)
entries.notes: Today's MUB-uh-shur stresses the first syllable. Pakistani and British Pakistani bearers dominate (wd PK; GB-EAW 176); Urdu short a → 'uh'.

entries.name: Rebeca
entries.source: Wiktionary, Rebeca: Spanish /reˈbeka/; Brazil /ʁeˈbɛ.kɐ/ [heˈbɛ.kɐ]
entries.notes: Spanish-speaking bearers (ES register 31.8k, Mexico, Latin America, US Hispanic 13.8k) are taken as larger than Brazil's 92k. Stressed open e → 'ay' (guide table, as José, Emre). Today's reh-BEK-uh is the English Rebecca vowel, close to the Brazilian [ɛ]. Reviewer: Forebears 2014 confirms it: Mexico 104,833, Spain 32,980, Peru 14,286, Cuba 12,705, Venezuela 11,652 and Tanzania 47,287 (Swahili also says reh-BAY-kah) against Brazil 78,512.

entries.name: Pir
entries.source: Wiktionary, English pir (a Sufi holy man): RP /pɪə/, GA /pɪɹ/; Persian/Urdu پیر (pīr, 'elder')
entries.notes: Today's lexicon reads it as the acronym P-I-R (passive infrared sensor); the acronym is written in capitals, so case-sensitive matching keeps it apart. Pir is mostly a Sufi title used before names in Pakistan (Pir Pagaro); the reading is the same either way. The tech-list clash is for the merge.
entries.word_check: gold has 'pir' read pˈɪɹ, the same as the name: kept

entries.name: Sabri
entries.source: Arabic صبري (ṣabrī): stress on the closed first syllable; a next to emphatic ṣ is a back 'ah'

alternatives.context: Turkish bearers (wd TR 82): sahb-REE, final stress

entries.notes: Today's SAB-ree has the 'cat' vowel. Maghrebi bearers (FR register 5k, Tunisia) plus Egypt are taken as the larger group; Turkey is the largest single Wikidata country, so this is a close call. Reviewer: Forebears 2014: Turkey 80,774 (final stress, with Iran 5.8k and Afghanistan 3.8k) against Sudan 23,203, Egypt 20,452, Libya 7,345, Indonesia 15,912, Malaysia 7,735 and India 7,597 (first-syllable stress); the two readings are about even, so it stays a close call.

entries.name: Haruna
entries.source: Hausa Hārūna (Aaron) and Japanese 春奈 Haruna: stress on ru (penultimate in English, guide); today differs only in the unstressed first vowel

entries.name: Cristiano
entries.source: Wiktionary, Cristiano: Brazil /kɾis.t͡ʃiˈɐ̃.nu/, Italian /krisˈtja.no/, Portugal /kɾiʃˈtjɐ.nu/; IBGE 2010: 195,807 Brazilians named Cristiano

alternatives.context: English commentary on Cristiano Ronaldo: kris-tee-AH-noh, today's reading

entries.notes: Brazilian bearers (IBGE 196k) outnumber Italy and Portugal together. Brazilian ti → chi; nasal [ɐ̃] → 'uh' (Juliana precedent). Changes how Cristiano Ronaldo (European Portuguese) is read in English text; review. Reviewer: Forebears 2014 confirms Brazil 210,110 against Italy 22,230 and Portugal 5,830 (Mozambique 13,920 and Angola 11,067 follow Portugal's reading).

entries.name: Raoul
entries.source: Wiktionary, French Raoul: /ʁa.ul/ (German /raˈuːl/); final stress, as today
entries.notes: FR register 13.4k dominates. British today's unstressed 'lot' vowel in the first syllable is only an unstressed difference.

entries.name: Hellen
entries.source: Spelling of Helen (English /ˈhɛlən/) used in the US and East Africa; today's reading
entries.notes: Reviewer: Forebears 2014 confirms it: Uganda 175,397, Kenya 98,216, Nigeria 47,042, Zambia 37,653 against Brazil 44,247.

entries.name: Lois
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Lois: /ˈləʊ.ɪs/; today's lˈOəs differs only in the unstressed vowel

entries.name: Cem
entries.source: Wiktionary, Turkish Cem: /ˈdʒem/; Turkish c is j
entries.notes: Today's SEM reads the c as in English.

entries.name: Earl
entries.notes: Ordinary word 'earl' (the title; 'Earl Grey', 'the Earl of...'). The given name sounds the same as the word; nothing to ship.

entries.name: Théophile
entries.source: Wiktionary, French Théophile: /te.ɔ.fil/; French names take final stress in English
entries.notes: Today's THEE-uh-file reads th as in 'thin' and -ile as 'file'.

entries.name: Wael
entries.source: Arabic وائل (wāʾil) [ˈwaː.ʔil]: two syllables, stress on the long ā; the hamza keeps the vowels apart (guide)
entries.notes: Today's WAYL is one syllable with 'ay'. Egyptian bearers say [ˈwæːʔel]; the 'ah' vowel and two syllables are common to all.

entries.name: Vasile
entries.source: Wikipedia, Vasile Alecsandri: Romanian [vaˈsile]
entries.notes: Today's VAH-sul drops the final syllable and stresses the first. Final e → 'ay' as Italian -e (Daniele).

entries.name: Hikmat
entries.source: Arabic حكمت (ḥikmat): stress on the closed first syllable; today's HIK-mut differs only in the unstressed vowel

alternatives.context: Azerbaijani (Hikmət), Uzbek and Tajik bearers, and Turkish Hikmet: final stress, hik-MAHT

entries.notes: Arabic bearers (wd IQ 12, SY 6) against Azerbaijani (AZ 10), which stresses the last syllable; Arabic kept as the larger group. Reviewer: Forebears 2014 confirms it: Syria 67,856, Iraq 9,907, Jordan 3,372, Lebanon 3,182 against Azerbaijan 8,991 and Uzbekistan 2,814.

entries.name: Jair
entries.source: Wiktionary, Jair: Brazil /ʒaˈiʁ/ [ʒaˈih], GA /d͡ʒaɪˈɪəɹ/; Behind the Name Spanish /ˈxai̯ɾ/; IBGE 2010: 152,403 Brazilians named Jair

alternatives.context: Spanish-speaking bearers (US Hispanic, Peru, Colombia): HIRE, one syllable

entries.notes: Brazil (IBGE 152k; Jair Bolsonaro) is the largest group; Forebears 2014 agrees (Brazil 181,592, plus Mozambique, Angola and Cape Verde, against Colombia 34,992 and Mexico 12,610). Today's ZHAIR is one syllable. US 'eer' written ɪɹ as Samir and Faqir (reviewer).

entries.name: Günter
entries.source: Wikipedia, Günter Grass: German [ˈɡʏntɐ]
entries.notes: Short ü [ʏ] has no English match; the 'book' vowel as for Jürgen (n0013). Today's GUN-ter uses the 'cup' vowel.

entries.name: Piet
entries.source: Wiktionary, Dutch Piet: /pit/
entries.notes: Today's PY-it reads ie as two vowels.

entries.name: Alia
entries.region: US, France, UK, Canada, Tunisia, Italy
entries.source: Wiktionary, Italian Alia: /ˈa.lja/; Arabic عالية (ʿāliya) stresses the long first ā; French Alia [a.lja]

alternatives.context: some US bearers, as Aaliyah: uh-LEE-uh

entries.notes: Today's AY-lee-uh fits no bearer group: French (FR register 5.2k), Arabic, Italian and Indian (Alia Bhatt) bearers say 'ah' with the stress on the first syllable. Reviewer: Forebears 2014: Iraq 77,911, Pakistan 49,266, UAE 43,787, Egypt 41,468 lead; Arabic ʿĀliya and Urdu Aaliya both say AH-lee-uh, while Kazakh and Tatar Aliya (Kazakhstan 25k, Russia 22k) stress the last syllable.

entries.name: Cécile
entries.source: Wiktionary, French Cécile: /se.sil/; final stress, as today; only the unstressed first vowel differs

entries.name: Ellie
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Ellie (rhymes -ɛli); today's reading

entries.name: Stewart
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Stewart: US /ˈst(j)uɚt/, UK /ˈstjuːət/; matches today's US and GB

entries.name: Talat
entries.source: Wiktionary طلعت: Urdu /t̪əl.(ʔ)ət̪/, /t̪ə.lɑːt̪/; Persian Iran formal [t̪ʰæl.ʔǽt̪ʰ], Tehrani [t̪ʰæ.lǽt̪ʰ]; Turkish Talat with final stress (Mehmet, Murat precedents); Forebears 2014: Pakistan 49,282, Turkey 15,071, India 13,031, Iran 9,628, Saudi Arabia 7,693, Uzbekistan 6,114, Egypt 5,075, Bangladesh 3,574

alternatives.context: Arabic طلعت (ṭalʿat, Egypt; usually spelled Talaat): TAHL-aht
Urdu speakers who keep the ʿayn syllable (Talat Mahmood): TUL-ut

entries.notes: Reviewer: the largest group is Urdu-speaking (Forebears: Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, about 66k), not Turkish (15k). Wiktionary gives Urdu both TUL-ut and tuh-LAHT; the stressed final 'LAHT' is shared by Urdu tuh-LAHT, Turkish, Persian and Uzbek, so the reading stands. Only Arabic (Saudi Arabia, Egypt) stresses the first syllable. Today's TAL-aht stresses the first syllable with the 'cat' vowel.

entries.name: Lorna
entries.source: CMUdict (today's source) LOR-nuh; the English and Scottish name (Lorna Doone); nothing contradicts

entries.name: Jozef
entries.source: Wiktionary, Jozef: Slovak /jɔzef/, Dutch /ˈjoː.zəf/; Forebears 2014: Slovakia 261,908, Belgium 50,633, Poland 16,398, Czechia 8,982, US 5,938

alternatives.context: Polish bearers writing Józef without the accent: YOO-zef

entries.notes: Reviewer: Slovak bearers (Forebears 262k) far outnumber the Flemish and Dutch ones (52k) the entry relied on; both say y and stress the first syllable. Slavic o → 'oh' as Josef (n0004), Tomáš and Miloš; the Dutch reading differs only in the unstressed vowel. Today's JOH-zef uses English j.

entries.name: Quentin
entries.source: Wiktionary, Quentin: French /kɑ̃.tɛ̃/, English /ˈkwɛntɪn/

alternatives.context: English-speaking bearers (US 41k): KWEN-tin (Quentin Tarantino, Quentin Blake)

entries.notes: FR register 128.8k (mostly born since 1980) against US 41k and few British bearers. French nasal ɑ̃ → 'ahn', ɛ̃ → 'an' (Jean, Alain precedents); final stress. Changes Quentin Tarantino and Quentin Blake in English text; review.

entries.name: Elhadj
entries.source: From Arabic al-Ḥājj (pilgrim title used as a given name in Senegal, Guinea, Mali): long ā; final stress as Ousmane, Mamadou
entries.notes: Today's il-HAJ has the 'cat' vowel.

entries.name: Brittany
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Brittany: UK /ˈbɹɪ.tə.ni/, GA [ˈbɹɪʔn̩.ni]; today's reading

entries.name: Metin
entries.source: Turkish Metin: Turkish names take final stress (Mehmet, Emre precedents); i is 'ee'
entries.notes: Today's MET-in stresses the first syllable.

entries.name: Faqir
entries.source: Urdu فقیر (faqīr) [fəˈqiːr]: q → k; the long ī takes the stress; Fakir precedent (n0012) fəkˈɪɹ
entries.notes: Today's FAK-eer stresses the first syllable with the 'cat' vowel.

entries.name: Hamad
entries.source: Arabic حمد (ḥamad): two short a's, stress on the first syllable; Arabic a → 'ah' (guide), as today

entries.name: Rafik
entries.source: Arabic رفيق (rafīq): the long ī takes the stress; Armenian Ռաֆիկ also stresses the last syllable (Armenian stress is final); q → k
entries.notes: Today's RAF-ik stresses the first syllable and shortens the ī.

entries.name: Clyde
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Clyde: RP and GA /klaɪd/

entries.name: Hélène
entries.source: Wiktionary, French Hélène: /e.lɛn/
entries.notes: Today's huh-LEEN sounds the h and reads the stressed è as 'ee'.

entries.name: Gökhan
entries.source: Turkish Gökhan (gök + han), phonemic spelling: k and h are separate; final stress (Orhan precedent, n0016, or-HAHN); unstressed ö → 'uh' (Ömer precedent, n0010)
entries.notes: Today's GAH-kun drops the h and stresses the first syllable.

entries.name: Momodou
entries.source: Gambian form of Muhammad; final stress as Mamadou (n0002, mah-mah-DOO), as today

entries.name: Viviane
entries.source: Wiktionary, Viviane: Brazil /vi.viˈɐ̃.ni/, French /vi.vjan/, English /vɪviˈæn/; IBGE 2010 census: 230,822 Brazilians named Viviane
entries.notes: Brazil (IBGE 231k) outnumbers France (FR register 52k). Brazilian nasal [ɐ̃] → 'uh' (Juliana precedent, n0006); final -e is [i]. Population call; review. Reviewer: Forebears 2014 gives Brazil 222,618 against about 145k French speakers (DR Congo 36k, Madagascar 24k, Belgium 19k, Benin 16k, Cameroon 14k, ...); with the FR register's 52k, Brazil still leads.

entries.name: Ugo
entries.source: Wiktionary, Italian Ugo: /ˈu.ɡo/

alternatives.context: French bearers (FR register 11.2k): oo-GOH, final stress
Igbo Ugo ('eagle'), Nigeria: same OO-goh, tones dropped

entries.notes: Today's reading has no stress mark. Italian bearers (wd IT 423) are the largest group (Hugo precedent).

entries.name: Fāṭima al-Zahra
entries.source: Arabic فاطمة الزهراء (Fāṭima az-Zahrāʾ): Fatima as n0002 (stress on the long first ā); the article al- assimilates to the sun letter z (az-Zahra)

alternatives.context: Classical Arabic, with the stress on the final long ā: az-zah-RAH

entries.notes: Today's fuh-TEE-muh AL-zair-uh misreads both words. Low: the stress of Zahra is unsourced; Maghrebi Zohra (n0014) is initial, Classical zahrāʾ final.

entries.name: Sergej
entries.region: Russia, Germany (Russian Germans), Lithuania, Belarus, Kazakhstan
entries.source: Wiktionary, Russian Сергей: [sʲɪrˈɡʲej]; Wiktionary German Sergej: 'a transliteration of the Russian male given name Серге́й'; Forebears 2014: Germany 20,424, Russia 20,262, Lithuania 4,468, Belarus 1,247, Slovenia 1,178, Kazakhstan 1,032, Uzbekistan 621, Latvia 497, Czechia 416, Croatia 248

alternatives.context: Slovene, Slovak and Serbian bearers (Forebears: Slovenia 1.2k): SAIR-gay, first-syllable stress

entries.notes: Reviewer: was Slovene/Slovak SAIR-gay from the Wikidata counts (SI 35). Forebears shows the Russian transliteration dominates: Russia and the Russian-German community (Germany 20k) plus the Baltics and Central Asia, about 50k, against about 2k Slovene, Czech and Croatian bearers. Final stress, as Russian. Today's SUR-gay fits neither.

entries.name: Dušan
entries.source: Wiktionary, Dušan: Czech [ˈduʃan], Slovak [ˈduʃan], Serbo-Croatian /dǔʃan/, Slovene /dúːʃan/; all stress the first syllable
entries.notes: Today's DOO-sun drops the š.

entries.name: Miodrag
entries.source: Wiktionary, Serbo-Croatian Miodrag: /mîodraɡ/ (falling accent on the first syllable)
entries.notes: Today's MY-uh-drag reads mi as 'my' and a as 'cat'.

entries.name: Alisher
entries.source: Uzbek Alisher (Classical Persian ʿAlī-šēr, Wiktionary etymology): Uzbek and Tajik stress the last syllable
entries.notes: Today's AL-ish-ur stresses the first syllable with the 'cat' vowel and reduces 'sher'.

entries.name: Emmy
entries.region: US, UK, Canada, Germany, Netherlands, Sweden
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Emmy: /ˈɛmi/; German, Dutch and Swedish say the same
entries.notes: English, German, Dutch and Swedish bearers together outnumber the French group.

entries.name: Friday
entries.notes: The day of the week, always capitalised in English text. Nigerian and Ugandan bearers say the name the same way; nothing to ship.

entries.name: Lori
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Lori: /loɹ.i/, /lɑɹ.i/; today's reading

entries.name: Matilda
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Matilda: /məˈtɪldə/; Spanish /maˈtilda/, Finnish /ˈmɑtildɑ/

entries.name: Imelda
entries.source: Wiktionary, Imelda: Spanish /iˈmelda/, Tagalog /ʔiˈmelda/; today's differs only in the unstressed first vowel

entries.name: Beau
entries.notes: Ordinary word 'beau' (boyfriend). The name sounds the same (BOH); nothing to ship.

entries.name: A'isha
entries.source: Wikipedia, Aisha: English /ˈɑːiːʃɑː/ 'AH-ee-shah', Arabic [ˈʕaːʔiʃa]; the apostrophe in this spelling marks the hamza between ā and i

alternatives.context: a common English rendering, stress on the i: ah-EE-shuh (as Ayesha, n0011)

entries.notes: Today's uh-ISH-uh stresses the i and loses the long ā.

entries.name: Beni
entries.source: Hebrew בני (Beni) and Swiss German Beni (short for Benedikt/Benjamin): first-syllable stress, short e, as today

entries.name: Lambert

alternatives.context: Dutch, Flemish and German bearers: LAHM-bert

entries.notes: Ordinary word 'lambert' (unit of luminance), and capitalised 'Lambert' in English text is mostly the surname (Miranda Lambert, Adam Lambert), read LAM-bert as today. Given-name bearers split between English and Dutch/German/French readings; no single group dominates, so nothing ships.

entries.name: Fredy
entries.source: Spanish Fredy [ˈfɾeði] (Latin American form of Freddy): stressed e in an open syllable → 'ay' (guide table, as José, Emre)
entries.notes: Today's FREE-dee fits no bearer group: Spanish-speaking (US 4.7k, Peru, Colombia), Swiss and French (FR 2.5k) bearers all have a mid e.

entries.name: Tanisha
entries.source: Behind the Name, English Tanisha: /tə.ˈni.ʃə/
entries.notes: Today's TAN-ish-uh stresses the first syllable.

entries.name: Mervyn
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Mervyn: RP /ˈmɜː.vɪn/, GA /ˈmɝ.vɪn/

entries.name: Rami
entries.source: Wikipedia, Rami Malek: English /ˈrɑːmi/, Egyptian Arabic [ˈɾɑːmi]
entries.notes: Today's RAY-my is the plural of 'ramus' (anatomy, botany), a rare, lowercase, technical word; the name is what capitalised readers meet, so it's treated as a name (guide). Finnish and Hebrew Rami also start RAH-.
entries.word_check: gold has 'rami'; kept: 'rami' (plural of ramus) is an anatomical term

entries.name: Edi
entries.source: Indonesian Edi (from Eddy) has the taling e and penultimate stress; Albanian Edi [ˈɛdi] (Edi Rama), Slovene and Swiss/Austrian German Edi (short for Edvin, Eduard) also stress a short e; Forebears 2014: Indonesia 529,204, Brazil 16,561, Iran 5,608, Mexico 4,584
entries.notes: Reviewer: Indonesian bearers (Forebears 529k) are almost all of them; the reading is unchanged. Today's EE-dee reads the e as in 'evil'. Brazilian bearers (IBGE 2010: 14.6k) say ED-jee. Medium: no IPA source for the Indonesian name.

entries.name: Brayan
entries.source: Behind the Name, Spanish Brayan: /ˈbɾa.ʝan/
entries.notes: Today's BRAY-un reads it as English Brian; the Spanish spelling says BRAH-yahn.

entries.name: Eliane
entries.source: Brazilian Portuguese Eliane [eliˈɐ̃ni], as Wiktionary's Brazilian Viviane /vi.viˈɐ̃.ni/ and Eliana /e.liˈɐ̃.nɐ/; IBGE 2010 census: 343,168 Brazilians named Eliane; Wiktionary French Éliane /e.ljan/

alternatives.context: France, Switzerland, Belgium (FR register 103k, mostly older): ay-LYAHN

entries.notes: Brazil (IBGE 343k) outnumbers France (FR register 103k). Brazilian nasal [ɐ̃] → 'uh' (Juliana precedent); final -e is [i]. Today's ee-lee-AN fits neither group. Population call; review. Reviewer: Forebears 2014 gives Brazil 354,875 against about 150k French speakers (France 51k, Burundi 28k, Madagascar 26k, Switzerland 10k, Belgium 9k, ...).

entries.name: Aristide
entries.source: French Aristide [a.ʁis.tid] (FR register 4.3k): final stress in English, as today

entries.name: Marissa
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Marissa: /məˈɹɪsə/

entries.name: Frederico
entries.source: Portuguese Frederico: Brazil [fɾedeˈɾiku]; today's freh-duh-REE-koh differs only in unstressed vowels (final o/u as Celso, Edson)

entries.name: Alison
entries.region: US, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Alison: /ˈælɪsən/
entries.notes: English bearers (US 117k, older UK, Ireland, Australia) outnumber Brazilian (IBGE 2010: 73k) and French (FR register 16k) ones.

entries.name: Cassandra
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Cassandra: /kəˈsæn.dɹə/, /kəˈsɑːn.dɹə/
entries.notes: The tech list (Apache Cassandra) reads it as the name does; nothing to change.

entries.name: Fahimeh
entries.source: Persian فهیمه (fahime): short a [æ], long i, final open e; Persian final stress (Fatemeh precedent, n0016)
entries.notes: Today's FAH-him-eh stresses the first syllable. Final open e → 'ay' (guide table).

entries.name: Ursula
entries.source: Wiktionary, Ursula: German /ˈʊʁzula/; English RP /ˈɜː.sjʊ.lə/, GA /ˈɝ.sə.lə/; Finnish /ˈursulɑ/; Tagalog /ˈʔuɾsula/

alternatives.context: English-speaking bearers (US 12k): UR-suh-luh, today's reading (Ursula K. Le Guin, Disney's Ursula)
Spanish (Úrsula), Finnish, Filipino and Swedish bearers: OOR-soo-lah

entries.notes: German-speaking bearers (wd DE 643, CH 128, AT 80; one of Germany's most common girls' names of the 1930s-50s) are the largest group (anglo_share 0.05). German s before a vowel is z. Changes the English-text readings of Ursula K. Le Guin and Disney's Ursula; review. Reviewer: Forebears 2014 confirms it: Germany 899,605, Switzerland 65,761, Austria 25,868 against US 34,573 and England 7,630.

entries.name: Sonny
entries.notes: Ordinary word 'sonny' (form of address to a boy). The name sounds the same; nothing to ship.

entries.name: Rachael
entries.source: Spelling of Rachel (Wiktionary: English given name, variant of Rachel); CMUdict RAY-chul, today's reading

entries.name: Oumou
entries.source: Malian/Senegalese Oumou (Oumou Sangaré), French spelling: both vowels 'oo'; final stress as Mamadou

entries.name: Ghislain
entries.region: France, Belgium, DR Congo, Côte d'Ivoire
entries.source: Wiktionary, French Ghislain: /ɡi.lɛ̃/, /ʒi.slɛ̃/
entries.notes: Today's GHIS-lun sounds the s and stresses the first syllable. Nasal ɛ̃ → 'an' (Alain precedent).

entries.name: Cody
entries.source: English Cody: KOH-dee (the app's gold dictionary, today's reading)

entries.name: Onur
entries.source: Wiktionary, Turkish Onur: /onuɾ/; Turkish names take final stress (Mehmet, Murat precedents)
entries.notes: Today's OH-nur stresses the first syllable.

entries.name: Jo
entries.source: English Jo: JOH (CMUdict, today's reading); Korean 조 Jo is also 'joh'

entries.name: Bridget
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Bridget: /ˈbɹɪd͡ʒɪt/; today's bɹˈɪʤət differs only in the unstressed vowel

entries.name: Enamul
entries.source: Bengali ইনামুল (Arabic inʿām al-): Bengali stresses the first syllable; the spelling's E reflects the Bengali [e]; Abul precedent (n0007) for Bengali initial stress

alternatives.context: Urdu/Arabic-style reading with the stress on the long ā: in-AH-mool

entries.notes: Today's eh-NAM-yul inserts a y and uses the 'cat' vowel. Low: no source gives the stress.

entries.name: Kareem
entries.source: Arabic كريم (karīm): stress on the long ī; Karim precedent (n0002) kuh-REEM

entries.name: Henryk
entries.source: Wiktionary, Polish Henryk: /ˈxɛn.rɘk/; ch [x] → h (as Spanish j, guide), y → 'bit'; matches today

entries.name: Augustus
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Augustus: /ɔːˈɡʌstəs/, /əˈɡʌstəs/; today's US and GB each match one

entries.name: Michaela
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Michaela: US /mɪˈkeɪ.lə/; Czech [ˈmɪxaɛla]
entries.notes: Today's my-KEL-uh has 'eye' and the 'bed' vowel. Row usage is english (US 53k), so the English reading wins by the guide's rule, but German and Czech bearers (wd CZ 197, DE 196, AT 135) may outnumber English ones; review. Reviewer: Forebears 2014: Germany 191,115, Czechia 82,533, Austria 35,949 against US 17,187 and England 16,419. German speakers alone (about 230k) are about three times the English-speaking bearers (about 75k with the US register), so only the guide's usage-english rule (its Michele example) keeps English here. Decision needed.

entries.name: Sahana
entries.source: Sanskrit/Hindi सहाना (sahānā, also a Carnatic raga): long ā in the second syllable takes the stress (Hindustani weight rule)
entries.notes: Today's 'cat' vowel is wrong for every candidate. Low: Kannada ಸಹನಾ (sahanā, 'patience') would stress the first syllable, and the bearers' language mix (US 2.8k, GB, IN) is unknown.

entries.name: Lucio
entries.source: Spanish Lucio [ˈlusjo] (Latin America; [ˈluθjo] in Spain) and Brazilian Lúcio [ˈlusju] (IBGE 2010: 56k); today's LOO-see-oh differs only by the i/y glide
entries.notes: Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking bearers together outnumber Italian ones. Reviewer: Forebears 2014 confirms it: Mexico 87,604, Brazil 60,298 (plus Lúcio 49,543), Peru 39,335 against Italy 34,697.

entries.name: Mitchell
entries.source: English Mitchell: MITCH-ul (CMUdict, today's reading)

entries.name: Putra
entries.source: Indonesian/Malay Putra ('son', from Sanskrit putra): u is 'oo'; penultimate stress; Putri precedent (n0010) POO-tree
entries.notes: Today's PUT-ruh uses the 'cup' vowel.

entries.name: Jassem
entries.source: Arabic جاسم (jāsim): stress on the long first ā
entries.notes: Today's JASS-im has the 'cat' vowel for the long ā.

entries.name: Nasim
entries.source: Persian نسیم (nasim, 'breeze') [næˈsiːm], Arabic nasīm: stress on the long ī, as today; the first vowel differs only in quality

entries.name: Juliette
entries.source: Wiktionary, French Juliette: /ʒy.ljɛt/
entries.notes: FR register 117.8k plus Belgium, Switzerland and Quebec against US 36k and GB 2k. ü → 'oo' (Julien precedent, n0008). Changes English-speaking Juliettes (Juliette Lewis); review.

entries.name: Benedito
entries.source: Wiktionary, Benedito: Brazil /be.neˈd͡ʒi.tu/, Portugal /bɨ.nɨˈdi.tu/; IBGE 2010: 214,024 Brazilians
entries.notes: Today's beh-neh-DEE-toh misses the Brazilian di → ji in the stressed syllable.

entries.name: Giuliano
entries.source: Italian Giuliano [dʒuˈljaːno]: stress on the long a
entries.notes: GB-only fix: British today says ʤˌuːliˈɒnQ, the 'lot' vowel for the stressed Italian a. US already right (li/lj glide only).

entries.name: Agatha
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Agatha: /ˈæɡəθə/
entries.notes: English bearers outnumber Dutch (/aːˈɣaː.taː/), Indonesian and Brazilian (IBGE 13k) ones. Reviewer: Forebears 2014: Tanzania 42,592, Brazil 42,388, Nigeria 42,193, Uganda 19,457, US 8,139; English-speaking African and US bearers together are the largest group.

entries.name: Ridwan
entries.source: Indonesian/Malay Ridwan: penultimate stress (Indonesian stress rule), as today

alternatives.context: Arabic رضوان (riḍwān) and Nigerian bearers: final stress, rid-WAHN

entries.notes: Indonesian and Malaysian bearers are the largest Wikidata groups (ID 7, MY 5); Arabic and Nigerian bearers stress the last syllable. Reviewer: Forebears 2014 confirms it: Indonesia 212,218 against Nigeria 34,660 and Somaliland 16,034.

entries.name: Sulaiman
entries.region: Nigeria, Saudi Arabia, Indonesia, Sierra Leone, Uganda
entries.source: Arabic سليمان (sulaymān) and Urdu سلیمان: the superheavy last syllable -mān takes the stress (Arabic stress rule; Hindustani weight rule)

alternatives.context: Malay and East African bearers: soo-LY-mun

entries.notes: Today's suh-LAY-mun reduces the long final ā and stresses the second syllable. Reviewer: Forebears puts Nigeria first (290k), then Saudi Arabia 157k, Indonesia 99k, Sierra Leone 43k, Uganda 41k, India 25k, Malaysia 18k; Pakistan has only 2.3k, so this is mainly an Arabic and West African name. The final-stressed long ā is the Arabic reading; Gulf colloquial Slēmān and the Hausa short form Sule support the 'ay' in the second syllable, but no source gives the Nigerian pronunciation, and Indonesian and Malay bearers stress the second syllable (alternative). Low.

entries.name: Aymen
entries.source: Arabic أيمن (ayman) [ˈʔaj.man]; Aymen is the Tunisian/French spelling (FR register 10k, wd TN 42); the diphthong is 'eye' (Ayman precedent, n0010)

alternatives.context: Egyptian and Levantine colloquial, where ay becomes [eː]: AY-mun (today's reading)

entries.notes: Today's AY-mun is the Egyptian/Levantine colloquial vowel; Tunisian bearers keep the diphthong.

entries.name: Chika
entries.source: Japanese ちか/知香 (Chika) [t͡ɕika] and Igbo Chika [tʃíká]: chi as 'chee', first-syllable stress in English, as today
entries.notes: Tones and pitch accent dropped.

entries.name: Kehinde
entries.source: Yoruba Kẹ́hìndé (yorubaname.com: kẹ́hìn-dé): ẹ [ɛ], nasal ì heard with an n, final é → 'ay'; English speakers stress the middle syllable (Babatunde precedent, n0014)
entries.notes: Today's kih-HIND reads -inde as 'hind' and drops the final vowel. Tones dropped.

entries.name: Jhon
entries.source: Colombian Spanish Jhon [ˈʝon]/[ˈd͡ʒon]: the Jh spelling marks an English-style j; Spanish o → 'oh' (guide table)

alternatives.context: as English John: JON, today's reading

entries.notes: The spelling imitates English John, but its Colombian, Peruvian and Ecuadorian bearers say a pure Spanish o (Brayan precedent in this batch: the Spanish reading of an English-derived spelling).

entries.name: Shadi
entries.source: Wiktionary, Persian شادی (šâdi, 'joy'): Iran formal [ʃɒː.d̪iː], classical /ʃaː.ˈdiː/; Behind the Name Shadi (2), Persian feminine

alternatives.context: the Arabic masculine name شادي (Levant, Egypt), SHAH-dee; n0019 chose this

entries.notes: Iranian (feminine) reading, stress on the suffix -i. Conflicts with n0019 (first-syllable stress, Arabic): pick one at merge.

entries.name: Alba
entries.source: Spanish/Catalan/Italian Alba ('dawn') [ˈalβa]; ES register 126k
entries.notes: Word 'alba' (a dawn poem; Gaelic name of Scotland), and capitalised 'Alba' in English text is mostly the surname Jessica Alba, read AL-buh as today. The given name's Spanish, Catalan and Italian bearers say AHL-buh (in us/gb), so a name entry would change Jessica Alba.

entries.name: Sonja
entries.source: German Wiktionary, Sonja: [ˈzɔnja]; Forebears 2014: Germany 235,793, Austria 30,542, Switzerland 24,933, Luxembourg 2,130 (about 290k German speakers) against US 60,926, Netherlands 20,836, Sweden 18,445, South Africa 18,182, Belgium 14,154, Slovenia 9,879, Croatia 7,945, Denmark 7,471, Serbia 6,579, Finland 6,088, Norway 5,605 (about 200k s-readings in all)

alternatives.context: English (US), Finnish and some Scandinavian bearers: SOHN-yuh, today's reading (Sonja Henie, Sonja Morgan)
Dutch, Swedish, Norwegian, Danish and South Slavic bearers: SON-yuh

entries.notes: Reviewer: was already-correct (SOHN-yuh) on the guess that the s-readings together outnumber German. Forebears says otherwise: German-speaking bearers (about 290k; a top name in 1960s-70s Germany) outnumber every other group combined (about 200k, and those split between 'oh' and 'aw' vowels). German s before a vowel is z; short o [ɔ] as Wolfgang and Konrad. Population call that changes English-speaking Sonjas (Sonja Henie); review with Ursula, Sabine and Susanne.

entries.name: Brianna
entries.source: English Brianna: bree-AN-uh (CMUdict, today's reading)

entries.name: Humphrey
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Humphrey: /ˈhʌmfɹi/

entries.name: Alassane
entries.source: West African name (Alassane Ouattara), French spelling: a's are 'ah'; final stress as for Ousmane (n0007) and Mamadou (n0002)
entries.notes: Today's AL-uh-sane reads -ane as 'sane' and stresses the first syllable.

entries.name: Eliana
entries.source: Spanish and Italian Eliana [eˈljana], English el-ee-AH-nuh; Wiktionary Catalan [ə.liˈa.nə]: the stressed vowel is 'ah'
entries.notes: Today's el-ee-AN-uh has the 'cat' vowel. Row usage is english; English, Spanish, Italian and Hebrew bearers share the stressed 'ah'. Brazil alone is a large group (182k); review.

entries.name: Constant
entries.source: French Constant [kɔ̃s.tɑ̃] (FR register 7.3k); nasal vowels → vowel + n, final stress
entries.notes: Ordinary word 'constant' (common, sentence-initial 'Constant pressure...'). The French name differs: kon-STAHN (in us/gb).

entries.name: Trisha
entries.source: English Trisha: TRISH-uh (the app's gold dictionary, today's reading)

entries.name: Arman
entries.source: Wiktionary, Persian آرمان (ârmân): Iran formal [ʔɒːɹ.mɒ́ːn]; Behind the Name Arman (1) /ʔɒːɾ.ˈmɒːn/ (Persian), /ɑr.ˈmɑn/ (Kazakh)
entries.notes: Matches n0019; Kazakh and Armenian bearers say the same. Today's CMUdict AR-mun stresses the first syllable.

entries.name: Al
entries.source: English Al (short for Albert, Alan, Alfred): AL, today's reading; the Arabic article al is said the same

entries.name: Jawed
entries.source: Urdu/Persian جاوید (jāved/jāwed): long ā, long e; the superheavy last syllable takes the stress (Javed precedent, n0016, jah-VAYD); this spelling writes the [ʋ] as w (Bengali জাওয়েদ, Jawed Karim)

alternatives.context: Tunisian bearers in France (FR register 1.7k), where Jawed spells Jawād: zhah-WED

entries.notes: The word 'jawed' (square-jawed) is rare and lowercase; the name is what capitalised readers meet, so it's treated as a name (guide). Today's JAWD reads it as the word.
entries.word_check: gold has 'jawed'; kept: 'jawed' (past tense of jaw) is rare

entries.name: Hind
entries.source: Arabic هند (hind): short i
entries.notes: Ordinary word 'hind' (hind legs; a female deer), and the Mi-24 'Hind'. The name differs: HIND with the 'bit' vowel, not the word's HYND; the name reading is in us/gb.

entries.name: Khoa
entries.source: Wiktionary, Vietnamese khoa: Hà Nội [xwaː˧˧], Huế and Saigon [kʰwaː˧˧]
entries.notes: Today's KOH-uh reads oa as two vowels. kh → k (Khánh precedent); tone dropped.

entries.name: Trinh
entries.source: Wiktionary, Vietnamese Trịnh: Saigon [ʈɨn˨˩˨], Huế [ʈɨn˨˩ʔ], Hà Nội [t͡ɕïŋ˧˨ʔ]; today's TRIN follows the Southern form, as Linh and Minh
entries.notes: Tone dropped.

entries.name: Aziza
entries.source: Arabic عزيزة (ʿazīza): stress on the long ī, as today

entries.name: Mildred
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Mildred: /ˈmɪldɹəd/

entries.name: Giancarlo
entries.source: Wiktionary, Italian Giancarlo: /d͡ʒanˈkar.lo/
entries.notes: Italian gia is 'ja' (Gian precedent, n0005); today's jee-ang-KAR-loh adds a syllable.

entries.name: Mỹ
entries.source: Wiktionary, Vietnamese mĩ (mỹ is its alternative spelling): Hà Nội [mi˦ˀ˥], Saigon [mɪj˨˩˦]
entries.notes: Today's MY reads y as in 'my'. Tone dropped.

entries.name: Trí
entries.source: Wiktionary, Vietnamese trí: Saigon [ʈɪj˦˥], Huế [ʈɪj˨˩˦], Hà Nội [t͡ɕi˧˦]
entries.notes: Today's TRY reads í as 'eye'. Southern tr → 'tr', as Trinh; tone dropped.

entries.name: Samaneh
entries.source: Persian سمانه (samâne): Iranian æ, â [ɒː] and final -e [e]; Persian nouns stress the last syllable (as Fatemeh and Zohreh, n0014/n0016)
entries.notes: No Wiktionary IPA for this name; reading built from Persian phonology like Fatemeh (fah-teh-MAY). Today's suh-MAHN-eh puts the stress on the middle syllable. The ES register count (23) is probably a romanisation artefact; Iranian bearers dominate.

entries.name: Haider
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Haider: /ˈhaɪdəɹ/, borrowed from Arabic حَيْدَر (ḥaydar) or Persian حَیْدَر (haydar)

alternatives.context: Urdu/Punjabi speakers who say the ai as [ɛː] (today's HAY-der); no source found

entries.notes: Matches Haidar (n0016, HY-dar). Today's HAY-der is CMUdict's. Jörg Haider and Haider al-Abadi are also HY-der in English.

entries.name: Tessa
entries.source: English Tessa: /ˈtɛsə/; Dutch and Italian bearers say the same

entries.name: Małgorzata
entries.source: Wiktionary, Polish Małgorzata: /maw.ɡɔˈʐa.ta/
entries.notes: Polish ł is w and rz is the 'zh' of 'measure'; stress on the penultimate. Today's mahng-gor-ZAH-tuh reads ł as l/n and rz as r+z. Polish a and o as in Michał and Tomasz (n0015).

entries.name: Ilyas
entries.source: Arabic إلياس (ʾilyās): long ā in the final closed syllable takes the stress; French Ilyas [i.ljas] and Turkish İlyas also stress the last syllable
entries.notes: Today's IL-yuz stresses the wrong syllable and voices the s. Bearers are mostly French and Spanish Maghrebi, Turkish and South Asian Muslims, who all stress -YAHS.

entries.name: Leyla
entries.source: Wiktionary, Turkish Leyla: /lejˈlaː/; Persian لیلا and Azerbaijani Leyla also stress the last syllable

alternatives.context: English-speaking bearers (US 10,077, UK, Canada) and French: 'LAY-luh', today's reading

entries.notes: Population call: anglo_share 0.06 and the top Wikidata countries are Turkey and Azerbaijan, where Leyla is a very common name. The Leila precedent (n0007) kept LAY-luh because that spelling's bearers mostly say it; this spelling is the Turkish/Azerbaijani one. Worth a review: it changes English-speaking Leylas (Leylah Fernandez spells hers differently).

entries.name: Milad
entries.source: Wiktionary, Persian میلاد (given name): Iran formal [miː.lɒ́ːd̪̥], Classical /meː.ˈlaːd/; stress on the last syllable
entries.notes: US today (mi-LAHD) already has the right stress; the GB reading MEE-lahd stresses the first syllable, so this is mainly a GB fix.

entries.name: Laure
entries.source: French Laure: /lɔʁ/; French r is English r (guide); today's LOR matches

entries.name: Elías
entries.source: Spanish Elías /eˈli.as/: the written accent puts the stress on í
entries.notes: Today's EE-lee-uz is the English Elias with the stress on the first syllable. Same reading as Elias (n0004) and Matías (n0013).

entries.name: Harald
entries.source: Wiktionary, German Harald: /ˈhaʁalt/; Norwegian /²haːral(d)/; today's HAR-uld has the same stressed syllable and consonants, only the unstressed vowel is reduced

alternatives.context: Norwegian bearers, who often drop the final d: 'HAH-rahl'

entries.notes: German final d is devoiced (t); the difference is minor next to the shared stress and vowels.

entries.name: Silvana
entries.source: Italian Silvana /silˈvaːna/, Spanish /silˈβana/: stress on -va-
entries.notes: GB-only fix: the app's British reading gives the stressed 'ah' the 'lot' vowel (sil-VON-uh). US is already right.

entries.name: Carlton
entries.source: English Carlton: /ˈkɑːltən/ (US /ˈkɑɹltən/)

entries.name: Janusz
entries.source: Wiktionary, Polish Janusz: /ˈja.nuʃ/
entries.notes: Mainly a GB fix: today's British reading has the 'lot' vowel (YON-oosh). US today is YAH-nuush, which differs only in the unstressed vowel.

entries.name: Clarisse
entries.source: French Clarisse: /kla.ʁis/; French names take final stress in English (guide)
entries.notes: French register 28,515 against US 1,491. French [a] is US 'ah', British 'a' (Damien, Jeanne precedent).

entries.name: Nemanja
entries.source: Wikipedia, Nemanja Vidić: Serbian [němaɲa]; rising accent on the first syllable
entries.notes: Today's nuh-MAN-juh stresses the second syllable and reads nj as 'j'. Serbian nj is ɲ, the 'ny' of 'canyon'.

entries.name: Ikram
entries.source: Arabic إكرام (ʾikrām, 'honouring'): long ā in the final closed syllable takes the stress; Urdu اکرام and Uzbek Ikrom also stress the last syllable
entries.notes: Today's IK-rum stresses the first syllable and reduces the long ā. Bearers: Maghrebi women in Spain and France, South Asian men in the UK; both say ik-RAHM.

entries.name: Malick
entries.source: French spelling of Malik, French /ma.lik/; Wiktionary, Malik: /məˈlik/ (US); French names take final stress in English (guide)
entries.notes: Same reading as Malik (n0001, muh-LEEK). Senegalese and Malian bearers (Malick Sidibé, Malick Sy) write the French -ck. Today's MAL-ik is the English reading of the surname.

entries.name: Alioune
entries.source: Senegalese Alioune, from Arabic ʿAliyyun; French spelling ioune = 'yoon' with final prominence; today's ah-lee-OON matches
entries.notes: Whether the i is a full syllable (ah-lee-OON) or a glide (ahl-YOON) is a matter of speed; the stress and vowels match today's reading.

entries.name: Mahamadou
entries.source: French spelling of Muhammad used in Mali and Niger; French names take final stress in English (guide), as Mamadou (n0002)
entries.notes: Today's muh-HAH-muh-doo stresses the second syllable and reduces the a's. Follows the Mamadou precedent (mah-mah-DOO); the Mande and Songhay languages use tone, so English stress is a convention.

entries.name: Devin
entries.source: English Devin: /ˈdɛvɪn/; US register 173,156
entries.notes: Covered by the tech list (Devin the coding agent); its reading is the name's English reading.

entries.name: Riad
entries.source: Arabic رياض (riyāḍ): long ā in the final closed syllable takes the stress; French Riad [ʁjad]
entries.notes: Today's US REE-ud stresses the first syllable; GB ree-AD has the stress but the 'cat' vowel. Emphatic ḍ is plain d. Same pattern as Ziad.

entries.name: Evans
entries.source: English Evans /ˈɛvənz/ (the Welsh surname used as a given name in Kenya and Ghana)

entries.name: Neelam
entries.source: Hindi नीलम (nīlam, 'sapphire'): long ī in the first syllable takes the stress (Hindustani stress rule); today's NEE-lum matches

entries.name: Konrad
entries.source: Wiktionary, German Konrad: /ˈkɔnʁaːt/; Polish /ˈkɔn.rat/
entries.notes: German and Polish bearers dominate (anglo_share 0.03). Both say a full 'raht' with a devoiced d (as Eduard, Ferdinand, n0006); today's KON-rud reduces it.

entries.name: Shalini
entries.source: Sanskrit/Hindi शालिनी (śālinī): long ā in the first syllable is the heaviest, so it takes the stress (Hindustani stress rule, as Nalini and Rohini)
entries.notes: Today's shuh-LEE-nee reduces the long ā and stresses the second syllable. Tamil and Malayalam bearers also stress the first syllable.

entries.name: Ziad
entries.source: Arabic زياد (ziyād): long ā in the final closed syllable takes the stress
entries.notes: Today's ZEE-ad stresses the first syllable and uses the 'cat' vowel. Same pattern as Riad.

entries.name: Reshma
entries.source: Hindi रेशमा (reśmā, 'silken'): first-syllable stress; e in a closed syllable is English 'eh' (guide); today's RESH-muh matches

entries.name: Oleg
entries.source: Wiktionary, Russian Оле́г: /ɐˈlʲek/; stress on the second syllable
entries.notes: Today's OH-lug stresses the first syllable. Unstressed Russian o is 'uh'; final g kept voiced, as Leonid (n0013).

entries.name: Fabián
entries.source: Spanish Fabián /faˈbjan/: the written accent stresses the last syllable
entries.notes: Today's FAY-bee-un is the English Fabian. Spanish b between vowels is soft [β], English b.

entries.name: Véronique
entries.source: French Véronique: /ve.ʁɔ.nik/; today's veh-ruh-NEEK has the same stressed syllable, only unstressed vowels differ

entries.name: Evelyne
entries.source: French Évelyne/Evelyne: /ev.lin/; French names take final stress in English (guide)
entries.notes: French register 127,795. Today's EV-il-ine reads it like English Evelyn with -ine. Many French speakers keep a light schwa (ev-uh-LEEN).

entries.name: Gokul
entries.source: Sanskrit गोकुल (gokula): long o in the first syllable takes the stress; today's GOH-kul differs only in the unstressed vowel

entries.name: Sanchita
entries.source: Sanskrit/Hindi संचिता (sañcitā): the closed first syllable takes the stress (Hindustani stress rule, as Sanjana, n0012); c is 'ch'
entries.notes: Today's sahn-KEE-tuh reads ch as k. Hindi and Bengali bearers both use it; I found no count to say which is larger, and no source for the stress. The 'ch' is certain.

entries.name: Sarojini
entries.source: Sanskrit सरोजिनी (sarojinī): long o is the heaviest syllable, so it takes the stress (Hindustani stress rule); Wikipedia, Sarojini Naidu: Bengali [ʃɔrod͡ʒini]
entries.notes: Today's seh-roh-JEE-nee stresses ji, which no group does. The pan-Indian reading follows the Hindustani rule; Bengali stresses the first syllable.

entries.name: Bachir
entries.source: French spelling of Arabic بشير (bashīr): long ī in the final closed syllable takes the stress; today's buh-SHEER matches
entries.notes: Only the unstressed first vowel is reduced.

entries.name: Sari
entries.notes: Ordinary word 'sari' (the garment). The Finnish name (SAH-ree) sounds the same as the word, so nothing needs shipping.

entries.name: Santos
entries.source: Spanish Santos: /ˈsantos/
entries.notes: Today's SAN-tohs gives the stressed a the 'cat' vowel. US bearers (19,334) are overwhelmingly Hispanic; Spain register 9,793.

entries.name: Moinuddin
entries.source: Arabic معين الدين (muʿīn ad-dīn), Urdu mu-ʿī-nud-dīn: the final long ī takes the stress (Hindustani stress rule: last of the heavy syllables)
entries.notes: Today's moy-NOO-din stresses the wrong syllable and loses the long ī of dīn. Many South Asian bearers glide the first two vowels (moy-nud-DEEN); I found no IPA for the name.

entries.name: Pappu
entries.source: Hindi पप्पू (pappū): short a [ə] in the closed first syllable takes the stress (Hindustani stress rule)
entries.notes: Today's PAP-oo uses the 'cat' vowel; Hindi short a is the 'cup' vowel (as Sanjay, n0001).

entries.name: Yūsuke
entries.source: Wikipedia, Yusuke: jɯːsɯke (ゆうすけ); Japanese names take penultimate stress in English (guide), which today's yoo-SOO-kay has
entries.notes: Japanese devoices the u of su, so natives sound closer to YOO-skeh; the guide's English convention keeps three syllables.

entries.name: Waldemar
entries.source: Wiktionary, Polish Waldemar: /valˈdɛ.mar/ (penultimate stress)

alternatives.context: German and Scandinavian bearers: 'VAHL-duh-mar' (today's US reading)

entries.notes: Population call: Wikidata counts Polish bearers (446) at twice the German ones (213), and Waldemar was a common Polish name in the 1950s-70s. German, Swedish and Norwegian bearers stress the first syllable. Worth a review.

entries.name: Adela
entries.source: Spanish Adela: /aˈdela/; Spanish e in an open syllable is English 'ay' (guide, as Josefa and Irene)
entries.notes: Spain register 23,159 plus Mexico and Argentina outnumber the US (11,342, partly Hispanic) and the Polish and Romanian bearers.

entries.name: Candy
entries.notes: Ordinary word 'candy'. The name sounds the same, so today's reading fits both and nothing needs shipping.

entries.name: Siarhiej
entries.source: Belarusian Сярге́й (Wikipedia, Siarhei Tsikhanouski: Сярге́й, stress on the second syllable); Belarusian г is [ɣ], romanised h
entries.notes: Today's SYAR-heej stresses the first syllable and reads the final -iej as 'eej'. Belarusian г is a voiced fricative; English speakers use h, as the romanisation does.

entries.name: Clinton
entries.source: English Clinton: /ˈklɪntən/

entries.name: Ferenc
entries.source: Wikipedia, Ferenc Puskás: Hungarian [ˈfɛrɛnt͡s]; Hungarian stresses the first syllable
entries.notes: Today's fuh-RENS stresses the second syllable and drops the t of c [ts].

entries.name: Abdurrahman
entries.source: Arabic عبد الرحمن (ʿabd ar-raḥmān): long ā in the final closed syllable takes the stress; Turkish Abdurrahman also stresses the last syllable
entries.notes: Today's ab-DUR-uh-mun stresses the second syllable and loses the h and the long ā. Same final stress as Abd al-Rahman (n0001).

entries.name: Sven
entries.source: Swedish/German Sven: [svɛn]; today's SVEN matches

entries.name: Jewel
entries.notes: Ordinary word 'jewel'. The name sounds the same, so today's reading fits both and nothing needs shipping.

entries.name: Cherry
entries.notes: Ordinary word 'cherry'. The name sounds the same, so today's reading fits both and nothing needs shipping.

entries.name: Hunter
entries.source: English Hunter: /ˈhʌntə(ɹ)/

entries.name: Nova
entries.notes: Ordinary word 'nova' (and Bossa Nova, Nova Scotia). The name sounds the same, so today's reading fits both and nothing needs shipping.

entries.name: Archie
entries.source: English Archie: /ˈɑːtʃi/ (US /ˈɑɹtʃi/)

entries.name: Tomáš
entries.source: Wiktionary, Czech Tomáš: [ˈtomaːʃ]; Slovak [ˈtɔmaːʃ]; Czech and Slovak stress the first syllable
entries.notes: Today's toh-MAHS reads it as Spanish Tomás. The á is long, not stressed, and š is 'sh'.

entries.name: Ifeoma
entries.source: Igbo Ifeoma (ife + ọma, 'a good thing'): i is 'ee', e is 'eh'; tone dropped, English stress on the penultimate, as Chioma and Ifeanyi (n0015/n0016)
entries.notes: Today's eye-fee-OH-muh reads the first i as 'eye'. Igbo ọma has open [ɔ], but English sources give 'oh' for it: Chioma (chee-OH-muh, n0016) and Ijeoma Oluo (/iˈdʒoʊmə/, Wikipedia).

entries.name: Tesfaye
entries.source: Wikipedia, Tesfaye: Amharic ተስፋዬ, tɛsfäyɛ ('my hope'), three syllables; the name site NameDrop gives tes-FA-ye
entries.notes: Today's TES-fay drops the final syllable. Amharic stress is weak; the second-syllable stress is the usual English rendering (name site), not a dictionary fact.

entries.name: Azhar
entries.source: Arabic أزهر (ʾazhar, 'radiant'): no long vowel, so the heavy penultimate az- takes the stress; Urdu and Malay also stress the first syllable
entries.notes: Today's uh-ZAR stresses the second syllable and drops the h.

entries.name: Alfons
entries.source: German Alfons: /ˈalfɔns/; Dutch and Polish also stress the first syllable
entries.notes: Today's AHL-fohnz uses English 'oh' and a z; German s is voiceless here. GB today has the 'lot' vowel in the stressed syllable.

entries.name: Damilola
entries.source: Yoruba Dámilọ́lá ('make me wealthy', ọlá 'wealth'): ọ is open [ɔ]; tone dropped, English stress on the penultimate (as Abiola, n0017)
entries.notes: Today's dah-mee-LOH-luh uses the closed 'oh'; Yoruba ọ is the open 'aw', as in Abiola.

entries.name: Clive
entries.source: English Clive: /klaɪv/

entries.name: Ayo
entries.source: Yoruba Ayọ̀ ('joy'): a is 'ah', ọ is open [ɔ]; English stress on the first syllable (as -bayo in Adebayo, n0017)
entries.notes: Today's AY-oh reads the a as 'ay'.

entries.name: Mahbub
entries.source: Arabic محبوب (maḥbūb, 'beloved'): long ū in the final closed syllable takes the stress
entries.notes: Today's MAH-bub stresses the first syllable, drops the h and shortens the ū. Same pattern as Mahmud (n0007).

entries.name: Olusegun
entries.source: Wikipedia, Olusegun Obasanjo: Yoruba Olúṣẹ́gun [ōlúʃɛ́ɡũ̄]; ṣ is 'sh', ẹ is open 'eh'; tone dropped, English stress on the penultimate (as Babatunde, n0014)
entries.notes: Today's oh-LOO-sig-un reads ṣ as s and ẹ as 'i'. The IPA is sourced; the English stress follows the batch convention.

entries.name: Rubens
entries.notes: In English text 'Rubens' is mostly the painter Peter Paul Rubens (ROO-binz, today's reading). The Brazilian given name (Rubens Barrichello, Portuguese [ˈʁubẽs]) differs only in the unstressed vowel and final s, so keeping today's reading for both is safe; name reading in us/gb.

entries.name: Maïmouna
entries.source: French spelling of Arabic ميمونة (maymūna): the long ū takes the stress; ï marks a separate i, giving 'my'
entries.notes: Today's MAY-moo-nuh stresses the first syllable and reads ai as 'ay'. Penultimate stress as Aminata (n0006).

entries.name: Caetano
entries.source: Wikipedia, Caetano Veloso: Brazilian Portuguese [kajˈtɐnu]
entries.notes: Today's kuh-TAH-noh drops the ae diphthong and uses English 'oh' for the final o, which Portuguese reduces to 'oo' (as Diogo, n0016).

entries.name: Jacinta
entries.source: Spanish Jacinta: /xaˈθinta/ (Spain), /xaˈsinta/ (Latin America); same pattern as Jacinto (n0012)

alternatives.context: Irish, Australian and other English-speaking bearers (Ireland register 1,665): 'juh-SIN-tuh' (today's reading)

entries.notes: Population call: Spain register 4,093 plus Latin America outnumber Ireland (1,665) and the English-speaking share of the US count. Spanish j is English h; Latin American seseo (s) is the larger Spanish group.

entries.name: Maximilian
entries.source: English Maximilian: /ˌmæksɪˈmɪliən/; usage english, so the English reading stays (guide)
entries.notes: Flag: anglo_share is 0.14, and Maximilian has been a top-10 name in Germany and Austria, so German-speaking bearers may outnumber English-speaking ones. The guide keeps the English reading for usage english rows (Michele precedent); a population review could switch it.

entries.name: Youcef
entries.source: Algerian French spelling of Yusuf; same reading as Youssef (n0006, YOO-sef), today's reading

entries.name: Laetitia
entries.source: French Lætitia/Laetitia: /le.ti.sja/; French names take final stress in English (guide)
entries.notes: French register 132,220 against US 353 and UK 161.

entries.name: Nazar
entries.source: Ukrainian Наза́р: stress on the second syllable; today's nah-ZAR matches (GB differs only in the unstressed vowel)

entries.name: Sherman
entries.source: English Sherman: /ˈʃɜːmən/ (US /ˈʃɝmən/)

entries.name: Amani
entries.region: US, UK, Egypt, Tunisia, East Africa
entries.source: Arabic أماني (ʾamānī): the long ā in the middle takes the stress; Swahili amani ('peace') has penultimate stress
entries.notes: GB-only fix: the app's British reading gives the stressed 'ah' the 'lot' vowel (ah-MON-ee). US is already right.

entries.name: Jacek
entries.source: Wiktionary, Polish Jacek: /ˈja.t͡sɛk/
entries.notes: Today's JAH-chek reads j as English j and c as ch; Polish j is 'y' and c is 'ts'.

entries.name: Camilla
entries.source: English Camilla: /kəˈmɪlə/; Norwegian and Danish bearers also have a short i (ka-MIL-la); only unstressed vowels differ

entries.name: Uğur
entries.source: Wikipedia, Uğur Şahin: Turkish [uˈuɾ]; ğ is silent between the vowels, stress on the last syllable
entries.notes: Today's YOO-gur reads ğ as g. Turkish u is 'oo'; the second u before r is the 'oor' of 'tour'.

entries.name: Fabrizio
entries.source: Italian Fabrizio: /faˈbrit.t͡sjo/; today's fah-BREET-see-oh has the same stressed syllable (zio as two vowels, as Fabio, n0006)
entries.notes: GB differs from US only in unstressed vowels.

entries.name: Byron
entries.source: English Byron: /ˈbaɪɹən/

entries.name: Katia
entries.source: Italian Katia [ˈkaːtja], Greek Κάτια; French /ka.tja/ (Wiktionary) has no lexical stress; initial stress as Nadia (n0002)
entries.notes: GB-only fix: the British reading gives the stressed 'ah' the 'lot' vowel (KOT-ee-uh). US is already right.

entries.name: Jeannine
entries.source: French Jeannine: /ʒa.nin/ (as Janine, Wiktionary French /ʒa.nin/); French names take final stress in English (guide)
entries.notes: Today's JEEN-ine fits no group. French register 198,140 against US 23,958. French [a] is US 'ah', British 'a' (Jeanne, Damien precedent).

entries.name: Yacouba
entries.source: French spelling of Yaʿqūb used in Ivory Coast and Burkina Faso: the long ū takes the stress; today's yuh-KOO-buh matches
entries.notes: Only unstressed vowels are reduced.

entries.name: Liza
entries.source: Russian Ли́за [ˈlʲizə]; Dutch, Greek, Hungarian and many US bearers also say LEE-zuh, today's reading

entries.name: Leonor
entries.source: Spanish Leonor: /le.oˈnoɾ/; stress on the last syllable (as Leonel, n0011)
entries.notes: Today's LEE-uh-ner stresses the first syllable. Spain register 20,105.

entries.name: Elmer
entries.source: English Elmer: /ˈɛlmə(ɹ)/

entries.name: Kwabena
entries.source: Akan day name for a boy born on Tuesday: Akan e is close [e], 'ay' in an open syllable (guide); tone dropped, English stress on the penultimate, as Kwame (n0017)
entries.notes: Today's kwah-BEN-uh has the right stress; only the stressed vowel changes (eh to ay). No IPA source found; the vowel follows Akan orthography.

entries.name: Iraj
entries.source: Wiktionary, Persian ایرج (iraj): Iran formal [ʔiː.ɹæd͡ʒ̥], classical /ʔiː.ˈrad͡ʒ/
entries.notes: Matches n0020. Today's EYE-ruj reads the long ī as 'eye'.

entries.name: Slamet
entries.source: Javanese slamet ('safe'): Indonesian/Javanese a is 'ah' and e here is the schwa; penultimate stress (regular orthography)
entries.notes: Today's SLAM-it uses the 'cat' vowel.

entries.name: Katarina
entries.source: Swedish Katarina /kataˈriːna/; Serbo-Croatian Katarina also stresses -ri-; same as Katharina (n0016)
entries.notes: GB-only fix: the British reading has the 'lot' vowel in the first syllable (as Katharina). US is already right.

entries.name: Brice
entries.source: French Brice: /bʁis/
entries.notes: Population call: French register 28,125 plus Cameroon, Ivory Coast and Belgium against US 15,477. Worth a review, like Damien (n0014).

entries.name: Iwan
entries.source: Wikipedia, Iwan Rheon: Welsh [ˈɪu.an]; Dutch and Indonesian Iwan is EE-wahn; today's EE-wahn matches
entries.notes: GB today has the 'lot' vowel in the unstressed second syllable only.

entries.name: Lars
entries.source: Wiktionary, Norwegian Lars: /laːrs/, /laːʂ/
entries.notes: Today's LARZ voices the s, as English 'cars'. Scandinavian bearers (anglo_share 0.03) say a voiceless s, or fuse rs into 'sh' (LAHSH); 'LARSS' is the English approximation.

entries.name: Edgard
entries.source: French Edgard: /ɛd.ɡaʁ/ (final d silent); French names take final stress in English (guide)
entries.notes: Today's ED-gurd reads it as English Edgar with a d. French register 3,860 plus Belgium against US 1,381.

entries.name: Abir
entries.source: Arabic عبير (ʿabīr, 'fragrance'): long ī in the final closed syllable takes the stress; today's uh-BEER matches
entries.notes: Only the unstressed first vowel is reduced.

entries.name: Fabiola
entries.source: Spanish Fabiola /faˈbjola/, Italian /faˈbjɔːla/; today's fah-bee-OH-luh has the same stressed syllable (i as a vowel, as Fabio, n0006)
entries.notes: GB differs only in unstressed vowels.

entries.name: Inna
entries.source: Russian И́нна: stressed и is [i]
entries.notes: Today's IN-uh uses the short English 'bit' vowel; Russian и is 'ee'.

entries.name: Todd
entries.source: English Todd: /tɒd/ (US /tɑd/)

entries.name: Brett
entries.source: English Brett: /bɹɛt/

entries.name: Salomon
entries.source: Wiktionary, French Salomon: /sa.lo.mɔ̃/; Old Spanish /saloˈmon/ (modern Salomón); French names take final stress in English (guide)
entries.notes: Population call: French (1,220), Spanish (723) and probably most US (3,574, largely Hispanic) bearers stress the last syllable; Dutch, Swedish, German and Finnish bearers the first. Today's SAL-uh-mun is the English Solomon pattern.

entries.name: Marsha
entries.source: English Marsha: /ˈmɑːʃə/ (US /ˈmɑɹʃə/)

entries.name: Nila
entries.source: Indonesian and Tamil Nila (Tamil நிலா, 'moon'): first-syllable stress with i 'ee'; today's NEE-luh matches

entries.name: Blake
entries.source: English Blake: /bleɪk/

entries.name: Delphine
entries.source: French Delphine: /dɛl.fin/
entries.notes: Today's del-FEE-nee adds a final vowel. French register 124,640.

entries.name: Saúl
entries.source: Spanish Saúl: /saˈul/; the written accent makes ú a separate, stressed syllable
entries.notes: Today's SAWL is the English Saul.

entries.name: Caitlin
entries.source: English Caitlin: /ˈkeɪtlɪn/

entries.name: Jill
entries.source: English Jill: /dʒɪl/

entries.name: Giovanna
entries.source: Italian Giovanna: /d͡ʒoˈvan.na/; same as Giovanni (n0003)
entries.notes: GB-only fix: the British reading gives the stressed 'ah' the 'lot' vowel (joh-VON-uh). US is already right.

entries.name: Abd al-Muhsin
entries.source: Arabic عبد المحسن (ʿabd al-muḥsin): muḥsin stresses its closed first syllable; ḥ is h (guide); same pattern as Abd al-Qadir (n0005)
entries.notes: Today's ab AL-muh-sin stresses the article and drops the h.

entries.name: Faiza
entries.source: Arabic فائزة (fāʾiza, 'winner'): long ā in the first syllable takes the stress, then i; Urdu فائزہ keeps the ā-i sequence

alternatives.context: a common quick South Asian reading: 'FY-zuh'

entries.notes: Today's FAY-zuh merges the two vowels into 'ay'. Maghrebi French spelling Faïza marks the same separate i.

entries.name: Lindsay
entries.source: English Lindsay: /ˈlɪndzi/

entries.name: Shamim
entries.source: Arabic/Urdu شمیم (shamīm, 'fragrance'): long ī in the final closed syllable takes the stress; today's shuh-MEEM matches

entries.name: Aïcha
entries.region: France, Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia, West Africa
entries.source: Wiktionary, French Aïcha: /a.i.ʃa/, /aj.ʃa/; Arabic عائشة (ʿāʾisha) stresses the long ā

alternatives.context: the two-syllable French and Maghrebi reading: 'EYE-shuh' (as Aisha, n0005)

entries.notes: Today's EYE-kuh reads ch as k. The diaeresis marks a separate i; the stress follows Arabic (as Youssef and Abdelkader in French spelling).

entries.name: Adolphe
entries.source: French Adolphe: /a.dɔlf/; French names take final stress in English (guide)
entries.notes: Today's uh-DAHL-fee adds a final vowel.

entries.name: Fazal
entries.source: Urdu فضل (fazl), said fazal [fəzəl] with an inserted vowel; first-syllable stress (as Samad, Urdu [ˈsəməd], n0018)
entries.notes: Today's FAY-zul reads the a as 'ay'. Urdu short a is the 'cup' vowel; the stress is not sourced (Fazlur, n0013, was left unresolved over the same question).

entries.name: Ashfaq
entries.source: Urdu اشفاق (ashfāq, from Arabic ishfāq): long ā in the final syllable takes the stress (Hindustani stress rule); q is k (guide)
entries.notes: Today's ASH-fak stresses the first syllable and uses the 'cat' vowel.

entries.name: Philomena
entries.source: English Philomena: /ˌfɪləˈmiːnə/

entries.name: Deng
entries.source: Wikipedia, Deng Xiaoping: Mandarin [tə̂ŋ]; pinyin eng is 'ung' (as Peng, Feng, Zheng in earlier batches)

alternatives.context: Dinka (South Sudanese) bearers of the given name Deng: 'DENG', today's reading

entries.notes: Decision to review: the given-name bearers here are partly Dinka (US 374, CA 88, AU, UG), who say DENG; but in English text the spelling is mostly the Chinese surname (Deng Xiaoping), which careful speakers say DUNG. Chosen for consistency with the pinyin -eng entries.

entries.name: Angélica
entries.source: Spanish Angélica: /anˈxelika/; Spanish g before e is English h, e in an open syllable 'ay' (guide)
entries.notes: Today's an-JEL-uh-kuh is the English Angelica.

entries.name: Günther
entries.source: German Günther: [ˈɡʏntɐ]; short ü is the 'book' vowel, as Jürgen (n0013); today's GUUN-ter matches

entries.name: Janine
entries.source: Wiktionary, French Janine: /ʒa.nin/; Dutch /ʒaː.ˈnin/
entries.notes: Population call: French register 63,035 plus German, Swiss and Dutch bearers (who use the French 'zh') against US 33,466 and the UK. Worth a review: it changes English-speaking Janines.

entries.name: Joséphine
entries.source: French Joséphine: /ʒo.ze.fin/; French names take final stress in English (guide)
entries.notes: Today's JOH-zuh-feen is the English Josephine; the accented spelling is French.

entries.name: Bahman
entries.source: Wiktionary, Persian بهمن (bahman): Iran formal [bæɦ.mǽn]; Behind the Name /bæh.ˈmæn/ (Persian)
entries.notes: Matches n0020. Today's BAH-mun drops the h and stresses the first syllable.

entries.name: Rico
entries.source: Rico: REE-koh in Spanish, Italian, German and English; today's reading

entries.name: Mikael
entries.source: Wiktionary, Swedish Mikael: /ˈmiːkaːˌel/; Norwegian /ˈmiː.kɑː.ɛl/; Finnish /ˈmikɑel/
entries.notes: Today's muh-KAYL has two syllables. Swedish, Finnish and Norwegian bearers outnumber the French register (17,560, partly Mikaël).

entries.name: Louisa
entries.source: English Louisa: /luˈiːzə/
entries.notes: French register 17,165 is a little below the combined US, UK, Irish, Canadian and Australian counts, and German bearers say it as English does.

entries.name: Hélio
entries.source: Portuguese Hélio: h is silent, é is open [ɛ], final unstressed o is [u] (regular orthography, as Diogo, n0016)
entries.notes: Today's HEE-lee-oh sounds the h and reads é as 'ee'.

entries.name: Tyrone
entries.source: English Tyrone: /taɪˈɹəʊn/ (US /taɪˈɹoʊn/)

entries.name: Ethel
entries.source: English Ethel: /ˈɛθəl/

entries.name: Daryl
entries.source: English Daryl: /ˈdæɹəl/ (US also /ˈdɛɹəl/)

entries.name: Sayed
entries.source: Wikipedia, Sayed Darwish: Egyptian Arabic [ˈsæjjed]; the ay diphthong is English 'eye' (guide, as Haidar)

alternatives.context: Urdu and Hindi speakers (सैयद): 'SAY-yed'; unsourced, see Syed (n0001)

entries.notes: Today's SADE has one syllable; every group says two. Syed (n0001) was left unresolved over the Urdu vowel; this spelling is mostly Egyptian and Afghan.

entries.name: Lotfi
entries.source: Arabic لطفي (luṭfī): first-syllable stress; the emphatic ṭ lowers u, which the Maghrebi spelling writes o; today's LOT-fee matches

entries.name: Rabia
entries.source: Arabic رابعة (rābiʿa): long ā in the first syllable takes the stress; ʿ dropped (guide)
entries.notes: GB-only fix: the British reading gives the stressed 'ah' the 'lot' vowel (ROB-ee-uh). US is already right.

entries.name: Nenad
entries.source: Wiktionary, Serbo-Croatian Nenad: /nênaːd/; falling accent on the first syllable
entries.notes: Today's NEE-nad reads the e as 'ee' and the a as 'cat'.

entries.name: Mumtaz
entries.source: Wikipedia, Mumtaz Mahal: Persian [mum.ˈtɑːz]; Urdu also stresses the long final ā (Hindustani stress rule)
entries.notes: Today's MUM-taz stresses the first syllable and uses 'cup' and 'cat'.

entries.name: Rashad
entries.source: Arabic رشاد (rashād): long ā in the final closed syllable takes the stress; US bearers (Ahmad Rashad) say ruh-SHAHD
entries.notes: GB-only fix: the British reading gives the stressed 'ah' the 'lot' vowel (ruh-SHOD). US is already right.

entries.name: Ephraim
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Ephraim (US): /ˈifɹi.əm/, /ˈifɹəm/, /ˈɛf.ɹəm/; today's EEF-rum is one of them

entries.name: Modibo
entries.source: Malian Modibo (Modibo Keïta): French /mɔ.di.bo/; English sources say moh-DEE-boh, today's reading

entries.name: Mamady
entries.source: Guinean/Malian form of Muhammad in French spelling /ma.ma.di/; French names take final stress in English (guide), as Mamadou (n0002)
entries.notes: Today's muh-MAH-dee reduces the a's. The Mande languages use tone; the final stress follows the Mamadou convention, not a source for this name.

entries.name: Yolande
entries.source: French Yolande: /jɔ.lɑ̃d/; nasal ɑ̃ is 'ahn' (guide); French names take final stress in English
entries.notes: Today's YOH-lund stresses the first syllable. French register 46,645.

entries.name: Inés
entries.source: Spanish Inés: /iˈnes/; the written accent stresses the last syllable
entries.notes: Same reading as Ines (n0016). Today's IN-iss is the English pattern.

entries.name: Florencio
entries.source: Spanish Florencio: /floˈɾenθjo/ (Spain), /floˈɾensjo/ (Latin America)
entries.notes: Today's flor-EN-chee-oh reads ci as Italian 'ch'; Spanish ci is s (Latin America) or th (Spain).

entries.name: Ghassān
entries.source: Arabic غسّان (ghassān): long ā in the final closed syllable takes the stress; gh is g (guide)
entries.notes: GB-only fix: the British reading gives the stressed 'ah' the 'lot' vowel (guh-SON). US is already right.

entries.name: Susanne
entries.source: Wiktionary, German Susanne: /zuːˈzanə/
entries.notes: Population call: anglo_share 0.08; German-speaking bearers (a top name in 1960s Germany) are the largest group, and Scandinavians also say three syllables. Today's soo-ZAN is the English Suzanne.

entries.name: Adeola
entries.source: Yoruba Adéọlá ('crown of wealth'): e is [e], ọ is open [ɔ]; tone dropped, English stress on the penultimate (as Abiola, n0017)
entries.notes: Today's ay-dee-AH-luh reads the a as 'ay' and e as 'ee'.

entries.name: Máximo
entries.source: Spanish Máximo: /ˈmaksimo/
entries.notes: Today's MAK-suh-moh uses the 'cat' vowel in the stressed syllable.

entries.name: Micah
entries.source: English Micah: /ˈmaɪkə/

entries.name: Ijeoma
entries.source: Wikipedia, Ijeoma Oluo: /iˈdʒoʊmə/
entries.notes: Today's ij-EE-uh-muh stresses the e and adds a syllable.

entries.name: Ademola
entries.source: Yoruba Adémọ́lá ('the crown joins wealth'): e is [e], ọ is open [ɔ]; tone dropped, English stress on the penultimate (as Abiola, n0017)
entries.notes: Today's AD-uh-moh-luh stresses the first syllable.

entries.name: Dick
entries.notes: Ordinary (and vulgar) word 'dick'. The name sounds the same (Dutch Dick is also 'dik'), so today's reading fits both and nothing needs shipping.

entries.name: Dian
entries.source: Indonesian Dian: i is 'ee', a is 'ah', penultimate stress (regular orthography)

alternatives.context: English-speaking bearers (US 5,549; Dian Fossey): 'DYE-un', today's reading

entries.notes: Population call: anglo_share 0.02; Dian is a common Indonesian name for both sexes. Today's DYE-un fits the US bearers.

entries.name: Antonius
entries.source: Dutch Antonius: stress on -to-; today's an-TOH-nee-us has the same stressed syllable, only unstressed vowels differ

entries.name: Adewale
entries.source: Wikipedia, Adewale Akinnuoye-Agbaje: Yoruba [ādéwálé], English /ˌædɪˈwɒli/ (stress on wa)

alternatives.context: the actor's own anglicised English reading (AD-ih-WOL-ee)

entries.notes: Yoruba vowels kept (e -> ay); tones dropped and stress put on wa, as the English IPA does. Same pattern as Adebayo and Babatunde in earlier batches.

entries.name: Shah
entries.notes: Also the English word 'shah' (the title: the Shah of Iran). The name is said the same way as the word (SHAH), and today's reading already gives it, so nothing needs shipping.

entries.name: Uche
entries.source: Igbo Uche (from uche 'will, mind'): u + che [tʃe], tones dropped; Igbo orthography is phonemic
entries.notes: Today's UCH (one syllable) drops the final vowel. Igbo e is [e]: 'ay' as in Emeka (n0013).

entries.name: Kunle
entries.source: Wiktionary, Yoruba Kunle: /kṹ.lé/; tones dropped, stress on the first syllable as English speakers say it (cf. Tunde, n0016)
entries.notes: Today's KUN-ul uses the English 'cup' vowel and loses the final 'ay'.

entries.name: Valentino
entries.source: Wiktionary, Valentino: English /ˌvælənˈtiːnoʊ/, Italian /va.lenˈti.no/
entries.notes: Today's reading matches the stressed syllable and consonants; only the secondary-stressed first vowel is anglicised.

entries.name: Alexia
entries.source: Merriam-Webster, alexia (the word): ə-ˈlek-sē-ə; English bearers say the name the same way; Wiktionary, French Alexia: /a.lɛk.sja/, /a.lɛk.si.a/
entries.notes: Collides with the rare medical word 'alexia', which is said the same way, so treating it as a name changes nothing. English (US, GB, CA) is the largest reading group; Spanish and Greek share its stressed syllable.

entries.name: Malaika
entries.source: Behind the Name: Swahili 'angel', from Arabic; Swahili stresses the penultimate syllable (ma-la-I-ka); Wiktionary Swahili malaika has audio only
entries.notes: Swahili orthography is phonemic and stress is penultimate. Today's muh-LAY-kuh merges a-i into English 'ay'.

entries.name: Slobodan
entries.source: Wiktionary, Serbo-Croatian Slobodan: /slobǒdan/ (rising accent on the second syllable)
entries.notes: Today's SLOH-boh-dahn stresses the first syllable; the rising accent puts it on -bo-.

entries.name: Nurul
entries.source: Malay Nurul (Arabic nūr al-): [nu.rul], first-syllable prominence
entries.notes: Today's nˈʊɹəl is NOOR-ul (ʊ before r, as in 'jury'); only the unstressed vowel differs.

entries.name: Elie
entries.region: DR Congo, Burundi, France, Madagascar, Cameroon, Rwanda, Haiti
entries.source: Wiktionary, French Élie: /e.li/; Forebears 2014: DR Congo 115,150, Burundi 36,206, France 31,886, Madagascar 29,928, Cameroon 23,100, Rwanda 22,721, Haiti 16,265 (francophone bearers, about 300k) against United States 5,872, Israel 5,693, Canada 2,774

alternatives.context: English and Lebanese bearers (Elie Wiesel, Elie Saab), EL-ee; Wiktionary English Elie /ˈɛli/

entries.notes: Reviewer: population call reversed. Forebears shows the spelling is overwhelmingly francophone (central Africa, France, Madagascar, Haiti); Lebanon is not in the top 20. French names take final stress in English; open-syllable é is 'ay'. Today's EL-ee (CMUdict) moves to alternatives. This changes how Elie Wiesel is read in English text: a decision for the parent.

entries.name: Larbi
entries.source: Maghrebi Arabic العربي (al-ʿarabī), contracted to Larbi, said LAR-bee; ʿayn dropped (guide table)

entries.name: Jens
entries.source: Wiktionary, Dutch Jens: /jɛns/; Danish, Norwegian and German j is the same [j]
entries.notes: Today's JENZ uses English j and z; Scandinavian and German j is the 'y' sound.

entries.name: Siavash
entries.source: Wiktionary, Persian سیاوش (siyâvaš): Iran formal [si.jɒː.væʃ]; Behind the Name /si.jɒː.ˈvæʃ/ (Persian)
entries.notes: As n0021 (plus a secondary stress). Today's SY-uh-vash reads i as 'eye'.

entries.name: Abolfazl
entries.source: Wiktionary, Persian ابوالفضل: Classical /ʔa.bul.ˈfazl/, Iranian [ʔæ.bol.fæzl̥] (final stress)
entries.notes: English speakers break the final zl with a short vowel. Today's AB-ol-faz-ul stresses the first syllable.

entries.name: Tommaso
entries.source: Wiktionary, Italian Tommaso: /tomˈma.zo/
entries.notes: Today's TOM-ah-soh stresses the wrong syllable. Geminate mm read single.

entries.name: Munawar
entries.source: Wiktionary, Arabic مُنَوَّر munawwar: /mu.naw.war/ (heavy middle syllable takes the stress); Urdu short a [ə]
entries.notes: Today's MYOO-nuh-wor adds a 'y' and stresses the first syllable. Urdu pronunciation not sourced directly.

entries.name: Josep
entries.source: Wiktionary, Catalan Josep: [ʒuˈzɛp], also [d͡ʒuˈzɛp]

alternatives.context: regional variant with a j sound (joo-ZEP)

entries.notes: Today's JOH-zep stresses the first syllable. ES register 40k: overwhelmingly Catalan bearers (Josep Guardiola).

entries.name: Hayden
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Hayden: /ˈheɪdn̩/

entries.name: Eman
entries.source: Wiktionary, Arabic إيمان: /ʔiː.maːn/; stress on the long final syllable; same reading as Iman (n0010)
entries.notes: Egyptian spelling of Iman (wd EG 14). Today's EE-mun stresses the first syllable.

entries.name: Saniya
entries.source: Hindi/Urdu सानिया/ثانیہ sāniyā (Sania Mirza): long ā in the first syllable takes the stress
entries.notes: Today's SAN-ih-yuh uses the 'cat' vowel.

entries.name: Jasleen
entries.source: Punjabi ਜਸਲੀਨ jaslīn: long ī carries the stress

entries.name: Marcio
entries.source: Brazilian Portuguese Márcio [ˈmaʁ.sju]; same reading as Márcio in n0011 (final unstressed o is [u])
entries.notes: Unaccented spelling of Márcio; bearers are mostly Brazilian (wd BR:118). Brazilian pre-consonantal r [h~ʁ] becomes English r.

entries.name: Dmytro
entries.source: Wikipedia, Dmytro Kuleba: Ukrainian [dmɪˈtrɔ ...]
entries.notes: Today's d-MY-troh stresses the first syllable and reads y as 'eye'.

entries.name: Farzana
entries.source: Urdu فرزانہ farzānā: stress on the long middle syllable (Hindustani weight rule)
entries.notes: Pakistani, Bangladeshi and British South Asian bearers. Today's far-ZAN-uh uses the 'cat' vowel.

entries.name: Michal
entries.source: Wiktionary, Michal: Czech [ˈmɪxal], Slovak [ˈmixal]; English (the Hebrew name) /miˈxɑl/

alternatives.context: Hebrew women's name, Israel and US Jewish bearers (mee-KHAHL)
Polish Michał written without ł in English-language records (UK, Ireland, Norway registers), MEE-hahw, as Michał (n0015)

entries.notes: Czech and Slovak bearers lead (Forebears 2014: Czechia 129,962, Slovakia 88,479; its Poland figure of 375,891 merges Michał). ch [x] -> h as Michał in n0015. Today's MICH-ul reads it as English 'Michael'.

entries.name: Agnieszka
entries.source: Wiktionary, Polish Agnieszka: /aɡˈɲɛʂ.ka/
entries.notes: Polish ni [ɲ] -> 'ny'; today's ag-NEESH-kuh reads 'ie' as English 'ee'.

entries.name: Mila
entries.source: Wiktionary, Mila: Italian and Spanish /ˈmi.la/, Serbo-Croatian /mîla/; English MEE-luh (Mila Kunis)
entries.notes: Lexicon (tech term) reading MEE-luh is also the name reading (Mila Kunis); no clash in sound.

entries.name: Aicha
entries.source: Wiktionary, French Aïcha: /a.i.ʃa/, /aj.ʃa/; Arabic عائشة /ʕaː.ʔi.ʃa/; same reading as Ayesha (n0011)

alternatives.context: two-syllable French and Maghrebi reading /aj.ʃa/, and the English Aisha (EYE-shuh)

entries.notes: Today's EYE-kuh reads ch as k. Bearers are Maghrebi and West African (FR 12k, ES 10k).

entries.name: Ferry
entries.notes: Ordinary word 'ferry'. The Dutch and Indonesian name is said the same way (Dutch [ˈfɛri]), so today's reading is right for both.

entries.name: Nafisa
entries.source: Arabic نفيسة nafīsa: long ī carries the stress

entries.name: Sheena
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Sheena: rhymes -iːnə (SHEE-nuh)

entries.name: Maciej
entries.source: Wiktionary, Polish Maciej: /ˈma.t͡ɕɛj/
entries.notes: Today's muh-CHEEJ is a guess; Polish ci [t͡ɕ] -> ch, ej -> 'ay'.

entries.name: Salima
entries.source: Arabic سليمة salīma: stress on the long ī
entries.notes: GB today has 'lot' in the unstressed first syllable; unstressed, so not churned.

entries.name: Caio
entries.source: Wiktionary, Portuguese Caio: Brazil /ˈkaj.u/
entries.notes: Today's KAY-oh gives the English 'ay' and an 'oh' ending; Brazilian final o is [u].

entries.name: Harvey
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Harvey: /ˈhɑːvi/, /ˈhɑ(ɹ)vi/
entries.notes: Lexicon (tech term) reading is the name reading.

entries.name: Bernd
entries.source: Wiktionary, German Bernd: /bɛʁnt/
entries.notes: Today's BURNT uses the English 'er' vowel.

entries.name: Manouchehr
entries.source: Wiktionary, Persian منوچهر (manučehr): Iran formal [mæ.nuː.t͡ʃʰeɦɹ], classical /ma.nuː.ˈt͡ʃihr/
entries.notes: h before r in the same syllable is dropped, as English speakers do (and Manouchehr, Mehrdad in earlier batches). As n0021 (plus a secondary stress). Today's MAN-oo-cher stresses the first syllable.

entries.name: Celeste
entries.source: Wiktionary, English Celeste: /səˈlɛst/; US register 61k is the largest group

entries.name: Agustin
entries.source: Wiktionary, Spanish Agustín: /aɡusˈtin/ [a.ɣusˈtin]; same reading as Agustín in n0008
entries.notes: Unaccented spelling of Agustín (ES register 56k strips accents; US 16k Hispanic). Today's uh-GAW-stin is the English Augustine pattern.

entries.name: Paulette
entries.source: Wiktionary, French Paulette: /po.lɛt/ (Spanish /poˈlet/); final stress in both, as in today's English paw-LET
entries.notes: French, Spanish and English all stress -LETTE; today's reading differs from French only in the unstressed first vowel (paw/poh), which the guide doesn't churn (as Valentina, n0007). Reviewer: Forebears 2014 gives France 84,767, Cameroon 9,300, Belgium 7,658 and Haiti 3,774 against United States 75,875 and Jamaica 7,069, so French bearers lead, but the stressed syllable is shared.

entries.name: Ayush
entries.source: Wiktionary, Hindi आयुष: /ɑː.jʊʂ/; long first syllable stressed
entries.notes: Today's EYE-ush merges ā-y into 'eye'.

entries.name: Anmol
entries.source: Wiktionary, Hindi अनमोल: /ən.moːl/; Hindi weight rule as in earlier batches (stress the heaviest non-final syllable, the last of tied heavies; CV.CVC takes the first): the long final syllable
entries.notes: Same stress pattern as Santosh and Pramod in earlier batches.

entries.name: Nuri
entries.source: Wikipedia, Nuri Bilge Ceylan: Turkish [ˈnuːɾi ˈbilɟe ˈdʒejlan] (first-syllable stress)
entries.notes: Today's nˈʊɹi is NOOR-ee (ʊ before r as in 'jury'), matching the Turkish stress and the Arabic nūrī, Korean 누리 and Indonesian bearers.

entries.name: Sinan
entries.source: Wikipedia, Mimar Sinan: Turkish [miːˈmaːɾ siˈnan]; Arabic سنان sinān [siˈnaːn]: final stress in both
entries.notes: Today's SY-nun reads i as 'eye'. Turkish, Arabic and Bosnian bearers agree on see-NAHN.

entries.name: Aadya
entries.source: Hindi आद्या ādyā: long first syllable stressed
entries.notes: US already right; GB-only fix ('lot' vowel today).

entries.name: Debi
entries.source: English Debi (Debbie, Deborah): /ˈdɛbi/; US register 3.8k

alternatives.context: Bengali and Odia Debi (Devi), usually inside compound names like Debi Prasad (DAY-bee)

entries.notes: The Indian estimate (wd IN 4) is the generic pool figure. Reviewer: Forebears 2014 gives India 52,185, Nepal 5,075 and Bangladesh 1,100 (DAY-bee, about 58k) against United States 28,936, Indonesia 18,511, Canada 2,034 and England 1,219 (DEB-ee, about 51k): close to a tie. Today's DEB-ee is kept because the groups are within the noise of the estimate and English-text Debis are mostly English-speaking bearers; worth a decision.

entries.name: Phuong
entries.source: Wiktionary, Vietnamese Phương: [fɨəŋ˧˧]; same reading as Phương (n0005)
entries.notes: Unaccented spelling of Phương. Today's foo-AWNG (CMUdict) splits it into two syllables with final stress.

entries.name: Pat
entries.notes: Ordinary word 'pat'; the name (short for Patrick/Patricia) is said the same way.

entries.name: Elham
entries.source: Wiktionary, Persian الهام: Iranian [ʔel.hɒːm], Classical /ʔil.ˈhaːm/ (final stress)
